section.title: The Sin of Favoritism
section.sectionRationale: James takes the pure religion just defined and tests it at the church door. Faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot coexist with fawning over the rich and shaming the poor. He exposes favoritism as an evil-hearted judgment, shows it contradicts God's own choice of the poor, convicts it by the royal law of love, and calls his readers to speak and act under the law of liberty, where mercy triumphs.
section.thesis: To honor the rich and shame the poor is incompatible with faith in the glorious Christ; favoritism breaks the royal law of love, makes us lawbreakers, and invites judgment without mercy on the unmerciful, for mercy triumphs over judgment.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the scene of favoritism exposed; God's choice of the poor and the folly of honoring their oppressors; and the royal law that condemns partiality and calls for mercy.

verses.text: My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show {{prosopolempsia|favoritism}}.
Suppose a man comes into your {{synagoge|meeting}} wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in.
If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,”
have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?

units.label: God's choice of the poor
units.note: you honor those who oppress you

verses.text: Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?
But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?
Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?
If you really fulfill the {{nomosbasilikos|royal law}} stated in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.
But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it.
For He who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker.
Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom.
For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. {{eleos|Mercy}} triumphs over judgment.

prosopolempsia.gloss: Partiality or favoritism, literally receiving the face, judging by outward appearance. It is the sin of showing deference to some and contempt for others based on wealth, status, or looks. James insists it cannot live alongside faith in the Lord of glory, who shows no such partiality.

synagoge.gloss: A gathering or assembly, the word behind synagogue. James uses it for the Christian meeting, reflecting the Jewish background of his readers. The scene of the two visitors takes place as the church assembles, making favoritism a public, corporate sin.

nomosbasilikos.gloss: The royal law, the sovereign or kingly law, love your neighbor as yourself. It is royal because it comes from the King and rules over all other duties toward others. To keep it is to do well; to show favoritism is to break it and stand convicted as a transgressor.

eleos.gloss: Mercy, compassion shown to those in need or at fault. James warns that the unmerciful will face judgment without mercy, then lifts the eye to the gospel note: mercy triumphs over judgment. Those who have received God's mercy are marked by mercy toward others.

basic.context: James gives a vivid picture. Two men walk into the church meeting, one rich and finely dressed, one poor and shabby. If you fuss over the rich man and shove the poor man aside, James says, you have become judges with evil thoughts. It clashes with faith in our glorious Lord. And it is backwards: God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while it is often the rich who oppress you and slander Christ's name. Favoritism breaks the great command to love your neighbor. And since God's law is a whole, breaking it here makes you a lawbreaker. So live as people who will be judged by the law of freedom, showing mercy, because mercy triumphs over judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is prescriptive teaching aimed at a specific sin, partiality in the assembly. The illustration in verses 2 to 3 is a hypothetical case, not necessarily a single reported event, used to expose a real pattern. A key point is verses 10 to 11: James is not saying every sin is equally serious in its effects, but that the law is a unity given by one Lawgiver, so to break it at one point is to become a transgressor of it as a whole.
basic.originalLanguages: Favoritism is prosopolempsia, receiving the face, judging by appearances. The meeting is the synagoge, the assembly. Love your neighbor is the nomos basilikos, the royal or kingly law. And the passage climaxes in eleos, mercy, which triumphs over judgment for those who show it.
basic.typology: The royal law of neighbor-love gathers up the second table of the Ten Commandments and points to its fulfillment in Christ, who loved perfectly. God's choice of the poor to be rich in faith prefigures the great reversal of the kingdom that Jesus announced. Mercy triumphing over judgment anticipates the cross, where mercy and justice meet.
basic.christ: James calls Jesus our glorious Lord, the Lord of glory, and faith in Him leaves no room for judging by outward appearance, for He judged no one that way. Jesus embodied the royal law, loving neighbor and enemy alike, and He announced God's blessing on the poor. Supremely, at the cross mercy triumphed over the judgment we deserved, and that received mercy is meant to flow out to others.
basic.god: God shows no favoritism and has chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom. He is the one Lawgiver whose law is a unity. And He is merciful, promising that mercy triumphs over judgment, while warning that those who withhold mercy will be judged without it. His heart is set against the proud partiality that despises the lowly.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus blessed the poor and pronounced the merciful blessed, Luke 6:20 and Matthew 5:7. Love your neighbor as yourself is quoted from Leviticus 19:18. Deuteronomy 10:17 says God shows no partiality. And Jesus warns that with the measure we use it will be measured to us, Matthew 7:1-2.
basic.oneStory: God has always taken the side of the lowly and warned against judging by wealth and status, from His care for the poor in the law to Jesus blessing the poor in the Gospels. James applies this to the church: to fawn over the rich and shame the poor is to deny the character of the God who chose the poor and to break the royal law of love. The gospel answer is mercy, secured at the cross, which triumphs over judgment and reshapes how God's people treat one another.

context.literary:
The section is a diatribe in the ancient manner, a lively argument conducted with an imagined listener, full of questions that expect an answer. It has four movements. Verse 1 states the thesis as a prohibition. Verses 2 to 4 give a scene, two visitors and two ways of treating them. Verses 5 to 7 break the scene open with three questions that expose the community's inconsistency: God chose the poor, you dishonour them, and the rich are the ones who drag you to court. Verses 8 to 13 turn to the law, where the single command to love becomes the measure, and the section ends on mercy.

The movement is a tightening net. James begins with a social offence and ends with the final judgment. Verse 4 says the favoritism makes them 'judges with evil thoughts', and verses 12 and 13 say they will themselves be judged. A listener who thought the matter was only about manners finds that the whole of the law and the day of judgment are involved.

There is also a deliberate echo of ordinary speech. The seat of honour and the 'stand' or 'sit at my feet' of verse 3 are the phrases a host would use, and James quotes them so that his readers recognise themselves. The paragraph closes with a pair of balanced sentences in verse 13, one about judgment without mercy and one about mercy winning, which gives the section its memorable end line.
context.historical:
The scene in verse 2 assumes a gathering, and the Greek word for meeting is the one that normally means synagogue. It may be that James is writing to communities that still thought of their assemblies in synagogue terms. In the synagogue and in the Greco-Roman world generally, seating signalled status. Banquets and public gatherings arranged people by rank, and a man with a gold ring and bright clothes announced his standing, and a ring and fine garments were ordinary signs of wealth.

The poor in the ancient world were often dependants of the wealthy, bound to them by debt and patronage. The courts were not neutral. A wealthy plaintiff could bring a poorer person to court and expect to win, which is the experience verse 6 describes with the word that means to drag. Prophets such as Amos had condemned exactly this, Amos 5:12, and the law had commanded impartial judgment, Leviticus 19:15.

The 'noble name' of verse 7 is the name of Christ, called over believers, possibly at baptism, and the rich in the readers' world may have used that name in mockery. Some of the rich may have been fellow believers, as in James 1:10, but James treats them as outsiders here. The readers' temptation was to court the powerful in hope of protection, and James reminds them where that road leads.
context.canonical:
Impartiality is a theme of the law. Moses commanded judges to show no favoritism to the poor or the great, Leviticus 19:15, and Deuteronomy grounds the command in the character of God, who shows no partiality and takes no bribe, Deuteronomy 10:17. Proverbs says that to show partiality in judgment is not good, Proverbs 24:23. The royal law itself is quoted from Leviticus 19:18, in the same chapter as the ban on favoritism, which James may well have in mind.

The New Testament repeats the point. Paul tells Romans that God shows no favoritism, Romans 2:11, and Peter learns it at the house of Cornelius, Acts 10:34. Paul tells masters to treat slaves in the same way because their Master in heaven has no favorites, Ephesians 6:9. The reversal in verse 5 echoes Jesus' blessing on the poor, Luke 6:20, and Paul's remark that God chose the lowly things of the world, 1 Corinthians 1:26 to 29. The royal law, taken up again by Jesus, Matthew 22:39, is called by Paul the fulfillment of the whole law, Galatians 5:14.

The close, mercy triumphing over judgment, belongs with the fifth beatitude, Matthew 5:7, with the parable of the unmerciful servant, Matthew 18:21 to 35, and with the line in the Lord's Prayer that links forgiveness given and received, Matthew 6:12. Judgment according to mercy shown is also what James affirms again at 5:9 and 5:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James wanted a congregation that was drifting toward a quiet class system to see how far it had drifted from the Lord it professed. His first words are not about the poor but about the glorious Lord Jesus Christ, so the issue is whether the community's practice fits its confession. A church that bows to wealth has made a statement about what it considers glorious.

He also wants his readers to see the cost. Favoritism is not a lapse of manners but a breach of the royal law, and it makes them lawbreakers whatever else they keep. He deliberately chooses a sin that many would call minor in order to show that no sin is minor against a God who gave one law. Finally he wants them to take up the posture of mercy, because they will themselves stand under the law of freedom, and mercy is what the merciful receive.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene in verses 2 to 4 is hypothetical. James says 'suppose', so it is an illustration rather than a record of an event. The commands of the passage are clear: do not show favoritism, love your neighbor, speak and act as those who will be judged. The remarks about the rich and the poor are descriptions of how things were for the readers, not rules for all places and times. The rich are not condemned simply for having money, and the poor are not praised simply for being poor; the passage is about how God has chosen, and how the community has treated them.

Application therefore asks for judgment. A church today may not seat anyone by wealth, but it can still favour by education, race, talent or usefulness. The principle carries over wherever people are weighed by what they can give, rather than by what they are in Christ.

debates.question: Does James 2:10 teach that all sins are equally serious?

views.label: No, it teaches the unity of the law
views.case: James argues that the same God who said one command said all the others, verse 11, so breaking any one is rebellion against the Lawgiver. He does not say that adultery and murder are equal in harm, only that each makes a person a lawbreaker. Elsewhere Scripture distinguishes degrees of sin, as in John 19:11 and 1 John 5:16.

views.label: Yes, in their standing before God
views.case: Others argue that any sin is enough to bring guilt and exclusion from God's presence, so in that sense all sin is equal. They find support in Romans 3:23 and Galatians 3:10, where one failure puts a person under the curse of the law.

debates.bearing: The text itself gives the first reading, since James only wants to show that favoritism cannot be dismissed as small. The second reading is a true point about guilt, but not what verse 10 argues.

debates.question: Are the rich of verses 6 and 7 believers?

views.label: Unbelieving outsiders
views.case: The rich blaspheme the noble name and drag believers to court. That is how persecuting outsiders act, so James is pointing to the ones the church is trying to please, who persecute it.

views.label: Wealthy members of the churches
views.case: Some think the oppressors included wealthy people in or near the assemblies, since verse 2 assumes a rich man enters the meeting, and 'your meeting' invites the wealthy as guests or members.

debates.bearing: Either way, the point is the same. The wealthy deserved no special honour from the church, and their behaviour showed that wealth was not the mark of God's favour.

debates.question: What does 'mercy triumphs over judgment' mean?

views.label: Mercy shown by believers is evidence that they will find mercy
views.case: The previous clause says judgment without mercy awaits the unmerciful. Mercy triumphs because a merciful life reveals that the person has received mercy, and so stands confident at the judgment.

views.label: God's mercy overcomes His judgment
views.case: Others read it more widely, as an expression of the character of God, who prefers mercy, Hosea 6:6, and who in Christ answers judgment with mercy. The believer who shows mercy shares that character.

debates.bearing: The two readings are complementary. The context favours the first, but the second explains why mercy is the right way to live.

study.originalLanguages:
The key word of the passage is prosopolempsia, in verse 1 in the plural, and the verb prosopolempteo in verse 9. It is built from prosopon, face, and lambano, to take or lift, and it translates the Hebrew idiom of lifting up the face, a phrase for acting on a person's outward standing rather than on the case itself. Paul uses the noun when he says there is no favoritism with God, Romans 2:11. The compound sets the face, the surface, against the truth of the person.

Verse 2 describes the rich visitor as a man with a gold ring, chrysodaktylios, literally 'gold fingered', in splendid clothing, esthes lampra. The poor man wears rhyparos clothing, a word of the same root as rhyparia, filth, in 1:21. James keeps returning to the language of dirt and cleanness, and so the poor man's dirty clothes are the same dirt the believer is told to put off, and yet the church treats the poor man as the one who is dirty.

Verse 4 asks whether the readers have not 'discriminated among yourselves.' The verb is diakrino, to divide or distinguish, which in 1:6 describes the man who doubts, driven and tossed. The same root links the favoritism of chapter 2 to the double mindedness of chapter 1: to treat people by rank is to be divided in oneself. The result is that they become kritai dialogismon poneron, judges of evil reasonings, or judges with evil motives.

Verse 5 uses the verb eklegomai, to choose for oneself, which is also the word used of God's election of Israel and of the Twelve. The poor are chosen 'in the world', to kosmo, which can mean either 'as the world sees them' or 'in the world's sphere', so that they are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, with a promise that is for those who love Him.

Verse 8 calls the law nomos basilikos, royal law. The adjective can mean either that it is the law of the king, the kingdom's law, or that it is the supreme law that rules the others. Both fit, since Jesus is the King who made neighbor love the second great command, Matthew 22:39. In verse 9 the favoritism is said to convict them, elegcho, a verb for bringing to light, so the law itself is the accuser.

At the end of verse 13 the final clause says mercy 'triumphs over' judgment. The verb is katakauchaomai, which literally means to boast against, to exult over. Mercy is pictured not simply as winning but as standing over judgment in triumph. The word is rare, and the only other place in the New Testament where it appears is James 3:14, where it describes boasting against the truth.

typology.type: The royal law and the King who fulfils it
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law was summed up in love for God and neighbor, Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, and the prophets looked for a king who would judge the poor with righteousness, Isaiah 11:4. Jesus is that King, and He names the two commands as the heart of the law and the prophets, Matthew 22:37 to 40. In Him the royal law is not only commanded but lived, and fulfilled at the cross, where He gave Himself for enemies, Romans 5:8. The correspondence is incomplete in that no believer keeps the law as He did, so James's royal law always drives us back to His mercy.

typology.type: The poor chosen to be rich in faith
typology.fulfillment: God's choosing of lowly Israel, not because it was greater than other nations but because He loved it, Deuteronomy 7:7 to 8, is a pattern of the way He chooses. Jesus announces that the kingdom belongs to the poor, Luke 6:20, and Paul says that God chose what is foolish and weak, 1 Corinthians 1:27 to 29. In Christ, who though rich became poor so that we might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9, the pattern reaches its centre. It falls short of a rule that the poor are automatically saved, since faith is still the means.

The law demanded judgment, and Scripture declares that God does not leave the guilty unpunished, Exodus 34:7. Yet the same God is merciful and gracious. At the cross judgment and mercy meet, since God was just and also the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25 to 26. This is the deepest meaning of mercy triumphing over judgment, not merely the shorter reading that those who show mercy will receive it. The correspondence falls short if it suggests that our mercy earns His. His mercy comes first, and ours is the fruit.

study.christ:
The passage begins and ends with Christ in the background. In the first verse He is called 'our glorious Lord Jesus Christ'. The phrase stands in a position that can be read two ways, as if He were 'the Glory' itself, which would make Him the visible presence of God that once dwelled in the tabernacle. If so, James is saying that the community has put a rich man in the seat of honour while the Lord of Glory sits among the poor. That is exactly where Jesus is found in the Gospels, born in a stable, dependent on others' hospitality, and crucified between criminals.

He is the one who showed no favoritism. Even His opponents admitted that He did not bow to men, Mark 12:14. He welcomed the poor, touched lepers, ate with tax collectors and received children, and He told the host who invited only the rich to invite the poor, the crippled and the blind instead, Luke 14:12 to 14. The man James describes as a lawbreaker, the one who defers to money, is the opposite of Him.

Jesus is also the source of the royal law. He called love of neighbor the second of the two great commands, Matthew 22:39, and gave it a new measure, 'as I have loved you,' John 13:34. When Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in this one command, Galatians 5:14, he has Christ's life in mind. In verse 10 James describes the impossible standard of the law, whoever stumbles at one point is guilty of all. That standard exposes everyone except Christ, who alone kept the whole law and then bore its curse for those who did not, Galatians 3:13.

Finally, the mercy that triumphs over judgment finds its centre in the cross. James says judgment without mercy will be shown to the unmerciful. Left on our own, all of us stand in that situation. The good news is that Christ was judged in our place, so that mercy might triumph for sinners, and those who have received this mercy are free to show it. This does not turn James into a gospel tract; it sets his warning in its right place, as the demand of a law that Christ has met and a Lord who gives mercy to the merciful, Matthew 5:7.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He does not judge by appearances. Verse 5 says He has chosen the poor, and the whole argument stands on the truth that His standards are not the world's. That is a repeated claim of Scripture, from Samuel's lesson that the LORD looks at the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7, to Peter's discovery that God shows no favoritism, Acts 10:34. He is a God who sees the person behind the clothing and who is moved by those the world passes over.

Behind the argument about the law stands a single Lawgiver. Verse 11 says the voice that forbade adultery also forbade murder, which means the commands are not a pile of rules but the expression of one will. That is why breaking one command touches the Giver of all of them. It is also why mercy matters so much: the law of love is not a lesser part of the law, but the royal law, the one that reveals what God is like.

He is the Judge, and He judges justly. The passage says that those who have shown no mercy will receive judgment without mercy. That is not an arbitrary threat; it is the way a God who is love, 1 John 4:8, and who requires truth in the inward parts, Psalm 51:6, deals with the heart. At the same time, mercy triumphs. The same God who judges with strictness is the one who prefers to show mercy, Micah 7:18, and who in Christ has found a way for mercy to be shown without making light of sin.

For worship this means that the way we treat the poor in the assembly is not separate from how we honour God. To lift the rich above the poor is to deny the God who chose the poor. To practise mercy toward the least is to join in His own character. The gathering of believers is meant to be a place where His impartiality can be seen, and where the Lord of glory is honoured by honouring those whom He loves.

crossReferences.note: The command not to show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich sits in the same chapter as the command to love your neighbor as yourself, verse 18. James quotes the second and applies the first. The law itself joins the two ideas that James is putting together.

God is described as one who shows no partiality and takes no bribe, and who executes justice for the fatherless and widow. This grounds the command in God's own nature. James asks his readers to imitate the impartiality of God.
Wisdom literature agrees with the law: to show partiality in judgment is not good. James is drawing on a deep stream of Old Testament teaching, and he writes as a teacher of wisdom as well as of law.

Jesus declares the poor blessed, for the kingdom of God is theirs. James 2:5 builds on this teaching, saying God has chosen the poor to inherit the kingdom. The echo of Jesus' words shows how closely James follows the teaching of his Lord.

Paul reminds the Corinthians that few of them were wise or powerful by human standards, because God chose the lowly things of the world so that no one can boast. It confirms what James says about the way God chooses and about the makeup of the early church.

Paul says God shows no favoritism. The word is the same one James builds on, prosopolempsia, so the command of James rests on a fixed fact about God. The truth is applied by Paul to Jew and Gentile, and by James to rich and poor.

Paul says the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree, love your neighbor as yourself. This explains why James can call neighbor love the royal law. Favoritism is a failure to love at the very point where love is most easily tested.

Jesus names love for God and love for neighbor as the two great commands on which all the law and the prophets depend. James follows His lead, quoting the second as the royal law, and treating it as the measure of how the whole law is kept.

Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. It is the clearest parallel to James 2:13. Both say that mercy given is linked to mercy received, which shows that James draws directly on the teaching of Jesus.

The prophet charges Israel with oppressing the righteous, taking bribes and turning aside the needy at the gate. James 2:6 describes a similar situation, with the courts used against the poor. It shows that his concern continues the prophets' protest.

Later in the letter James turns to the rich directly, condemning those who withheld wages and condemned the righteous. It fills out the picture of 2:6 and shows that his warning in chapter 2 is part of a wider concern for justice.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning the Bible teaches that every human being bears the image of God, Genesis 1:27, which is the deepest reason no person may be ranked above another. The fall brought pride, envy and violence into the world, and from the earliest chapters the strong have crushed the weak, as Cain did to Abel, Genesis 4:8. Against that, God's law gave Israel a justice that did not favour the powerful, Leviticus 19:15, and made special provision for the poor.

What the passage answers from before is the long failure of Israel's leaders to do justice. The prophets rebuked kings and judges for favouring the rich, Isaiah 1:23 and Amos 5:12, and promised a coming King who would judge the poor with righteousness, Isaiah 11:4. James writes in the light of that promise. The King has come, He has called the poor blessed, and His people are to be marked by an impartiality that the old world did not know.

What the passage sets up is the next argument of the letter. The whole law is kept in love, and faith that does not show itself in mercy is not alive, James 2:14 to 17. The warning against favoritism is the first example of the faith that works. Later the letter returns to the rich and the poor, 4:13 to 5:6, and to the mercy of the Lord, 5:11. The same concern appears in the way Paul speaks of the church as one body in which there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, Galatians 3:28.

The Bible ends with a multitude from every nation, tribe and people standing before the throne, Revelation 7:9, with no division by rank or wealth, and with the Lamb as their shepherd. There the gold ring and fine clothes have no standing, and the only robe that matters is the one washed in the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 7:14. The royal law is then perfectly kept, mercy has triumphed over judgment, and the poor whom God chose are seen to be the heirs of the kingdom He promised. Every church that welcomes the shabby visitor as warmly as the rich one is a small preview of that gathering.

quiz.q: Why is showing favoritism incompatible with the Christian faith?

options.text: Because it clashes with faith in the glorious Lord Jesus and makes us judges with evil thoughts.
options.note: Verses 1 and 4: partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory.

options.text: Because it breaks the royal law to love your neighbor as yourself.
options.note: True from verses 8 to 9, another angle on the same sin.

options.text: Because rich people should never be welcomed at all.
options.note: James forbids partiality, not the welcome of any person, rich or poor.

options.text: Because the church should simply ignore social differences.
options.note: James does not say ignore; he says do not judge people by wealth or status.

quiz.q: What has God done regarding the poor, according to verse 5?

options.text: Chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom.
options.note: Verse 5: God's gracious choice exposes the folly of despising them.

options.text: Blessed the lowly who trust Him rather than riches.
options.note: True to the sense, capturing the great reversal of the kingdom.

options.text: Promised to make every poor believer materially wealthy.
options.note: The riches in view are faith and the kingdom, not guaranteed money.

options.text: Rejected the poor in favor of the influential.
options.note: The opposite of what verse 5 says.

quiz.q: What does James mean by stumbling at one point of the law?

options.text: The law is a unity from one Lawgiver, so breaking it at one point makes you a transgressor of it.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11: the law's oneness, not equal consequences for every sin.

options.text: No one can claim innocence by keeping most of the commands.
options.note: True to the humbling effect, silencing partial-obedience boasting.

options.text: Every sin does exactly the same amount of damage.
options.note: James teaches the law's unity, not that all sins are identical in effect.

options.text: Small sins do not really count before God.
options.note: The point is the opposite: even one breach makes one a lawbreaker.

quiz.q: What does James say about mercy in verse 13?

options.text: Mercy triumphs over judgment, but the unmerciful face judgment without mercy.
options.note: Verse 13 holds both together: warning and gospel hope.

options.text: Those who show mercy will themselves receive mercy.
options.note: True to the thrust, echoing Jesus in Matthew 5:7.

options.text: Mercy means no one will ever face any judgment.
options.note: Judgment is real; mercy triumphs for the merciful, not by canceling judgment altogether.

options.text: God's judgment always overrides His mercy.
options.note: James says mercy triumphs over judgment, not the reverse.

quiz.q: What is the royal law James cites in verse 8?

options.text: Love your neighbor as yourself.
options.note: Verse 8 quotes Leviticus 19:18, the kingly law over our dealings with others.

options.text: The sovereign command from the King that governs how we treat others.
options.note: True to why it is called royal, though it names the principle rather than the words.

options.text: A rule that only applies to how we treat the wealthy.
options.note: It applies to every neighbor, which is exactly why favoritism breaks it.

options.text: The command to honor those of higher social rank.
options.note: That is favoritism, the very thing the royal law condemns.

questions: James pictures two visitors and how differently they are treated. Are there people you unconsciously honor or overlook because of appearance, wealth, or status?
God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith. How does that reshape the way you view people the world considers unimportant?
The royal law is to love your neighbor as yourself. Who is a neighbor near you that this command is calling you to love more concretely?
James says we will be judged by the law of liberty, so speak and act as merciful people. Where do you need to extend mercy rather than judgment right now?
Mercy triumphs over judgment. How does remembering the mercy you have received in Christ move you to show mercy to someone who has wronged you?

translationNotes.note: Meeting renders synagoge, literally your synagogue; a footnote notes the Greek, reflecting the Jewish setting of James's readers and their assembly.
The noble name by which you have been called can also be rendered the noble name invoked upon you, or the name of Him to whom you belong, that is, the name of Christ.
Royal law renders nomos basilikos, kingly or sovereign law; the quotation is from Leviticus 19:18, love your neighbor as yourself.
